HEADLINE: Punters have decided - it's a Coalition victory
INTRO: The election is over, according to the bookies.
TEXT:
The election is over, according to the bookies.

While stopping short of closing betting and paying out winnings ahead of polling day, betting agencies have decided the result is a foregone conclusion - the Coalition is heading to victory on Saturday.

Any hope of Labor picking up the 19 seats needed for victory faded about two weeks ago, and the odds of Coalition victory have firmed at the end of the campaign.

Three of the big betting agencies, Sportsbet, William Hill and Tabcorp, had this week put Labor at between $6 and $7 for an unlikely victory, while the Coalition was sitting on between $1.10 and $1.12.

Late on Monday afternoon, Sportsbet effectively called the election for the Coalition, shortening their odds to $1.08 and Labor's hopes drifting out to $8.

"They say it's not over until the fat lady sings, but looking at the betting she's already on the stage clearing her throat," Sportsbet spokesman Will Byrne said.

Sportsbet said they expected the Coalition's odds to shorten in the next few days, but books are expected to remain open until polling day.

"We've had 10 times the money on the Coalition versus Labor, but we've had three times as many punters backing Labor as they are chasing the better odds," they said.

"The first week of the campaign was Labor's best, shortening into $2.95, but it has been one-way traffic since with the big money heading for the Coalition. It [the Coalition's odds] shortening further."

Tabcorp said odds for a string of key marginals across the country had tightened for Coalition candidates. Big bets for the Coalition include $50,000 at $1.35 and $10,000 at $1.30 earlier in the campaign.

Punters are also betting on the return of One National leader Pauline Hanson to federal parliament.

Ms Hanson, who has unsuccessfully contested numerous state and federal elections since she lost her seat in the 1998 election, is having another crack at politics and is shaping up as a safe bet of winning a Queensland Senate seat.

Sportsbet has Ms Hanson's odds at $1.35, in from $1.60. Her main rival, former Palmer United Party senator Glenn Lazarus, known in his rugby league playing days as "The Brick With Eyes", at $1.87.

There is no shortage of categories for bets for Saturday night.

Crownbet is taking bets for the colour of Mr Shorten's tie at his post-poll speech (including $51 for black with CFMEU logo), the time former prime minister Tony Abbott will vote, whether Clive Palmer will be seen in his old seat of Fairfax on polling day or whether Mr Turnbull or Mr Shorten will cry during their concession speech if they lose.

HEADLINE: How to talk about politics
INTRO: It appears Australian voters are such socially awkward creatures that political parties and even private companies are offering conversational tips to help people navigate the last days of the eight-week election campaign.
TEXT:
It appears Australian voters are such socially awkward creatures that political parties and even private companies are offering conversational tips to help people navigate the last days of the eight-week election campaign.

Labor's "How to talk to a Liberal Mate" interactive website, the Liberal Democrats' "Freedom Flakes" breakfast cereal, and mobile telco Amaysim's "How to win on voting day" all offer the clueless handy tips on talking about politics without embarrassing themselves.

For politicians, there's a more prosaic reason behind the rush of online self-help political material.

The political advertising blackout begins at midnight Wednesday so while the mainstream media will be at last free of back-to-back attack ads, political parties have to find some other catchy way of persuading ordinary people to keep talking about the election.

Liberal Democrats senator David Leyonhjelm sent 20 boxes of his "Freedom Flakes" - as well as the less attractive "Bill's Shortana Bran" and "Malcolm Turnb'o's" - to breakfast program presenters on radio and TV to feast upon on Thursday morning.

In the weeks before the election was called there was barely a day Senator Leyonhjelm was not in the media talking about the Senate voting changes and other key legislation.

"But basically the interest in me as a senator just dried up as soon as the election campaign began," Senator Leyonhjelm said.

"It almost reminded me of life before my senate career began - nobody wanted to know me."

After early forays with Youtube videos of the senator cooking a fish in his shoe - to protest a proposed sugar tax - and his two pugs eating his superannuation nest egg - protesting both parties' super policies, the breakfast cereal plan is his last-ditch effort to remind voters that the senate is still important.

"There's only one party that has consistently voted for freedom and well, it [Freedom Flakes] is a gimmick quite frankly," he said.

Labor is taking a more direct approach, providing interactive cheat sheets for Labor supporters talking to their Liberal friends.

The party's head of digital, Erinn Swan, told supporters the election would come down to only a handful of votes so "a conversation you have with a friend could change their vote and change the election".

For example, Liberal Mate Says: Turnbull will be able to govern like a more progressive person once he wins an election.

Labor's recommended conversational response: "Bill Shorten leads his party - Malcolm Turnbull's party leads him. If anything, we are on track to see Malcolm Turnbull even more dominated by nutjobs and cavemen."

The private sector is taking a more bipartisan approach to the voting day conundrum.

Online financial comparison company, Finder.com.au, realised that with 1 in 4 Australians were uncomfortable talking about politics so it created a new online senate voting tool to keep track of the 100-plus senate candidates in some states without the embarrassment of asking polling booth volunteers for a how-to-card.

Once a voter has input his or her voting inclinations into the tool, it generates a custom how-to-vote cheat sheet they can bring on voting day.

It's a real-life variation of the telco Amaysim's how-to-vote parody video which urges the politically disengaged to bring their BYO political pamphlets, or better still just "avoid the whole thing" by making a postal vote.

HEADLINE: Small business cools on Turnbull
INTRO: Small and medium business owners have cooled on Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull just as he needs their votes, but they still view his government more favourably than the former Labor governments, the MYOB Business Monitor finds.
TEXT:
Small and medium business owners have cooled on Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull just as he needs their votes, but they still view his government more favourably than the former Labor governments, the MYOB Business Monitor finds.

One thing that could bring them around would be a promise to make the automatic $20,000 asset write-off for tax purposes permanent. Two-thirds of the more than 1000 small and medium enterprises (SMEs) surveyed named this as their top vote-changer.

"On the one hand the government remains far more popular amongst SMEs than its predecessor," MYOB chief executive Tim Reed said. "On the other, as the government lobbies for pre-election support from this crucial business sector, dissatisfaction levels in the past six months have increased."

The government has bent over backwards to announce policies to appeal to small and medium business folk such as raising the cap on eligibility for the instant asset write-off to firms with turnover of $10 million, tax cuts and youth employment incentives.

"I'm sure it is concerning that despite an election campaign that has placed a significant amount of attention on business, the results show the government's message isn't resonating as strongly as they'd like," Mr Reed said.

The latest MYOB Business Monitor shows the percentage of SMEs who feel "totally dissatisfied" with the government - 32 per cent - again exceeds the 20 per cent who feel "totally satisfied".

Only last October, just after Mr Turnbull replaced Tony Abbott as Prime Minister, positive assessments outweighed negative assessments 30 per cent to 26 per cent. During the Rudd and Gillard governments, "totally dissatisfied" small business hit 57 per cent and "totally satisfied" respondents plumbed 11 per cent.

State governments also get a bad rap; negative views jumped from 30 per cent in October to 38 per cent.

Bright spots for the Turnbull government are young business owners, who are more satisfied than baby boomer business owners, and sole traders.

Other policies small business would vote for include a guaranteed share of government contracts, incentives to employ over 50s, and more funding for skills, training and apprenticeships.

At the start of the election campaign they told MYOB they saw the election as a chance to cut red tape and tax, boost confidence and return a government with a workable Senate majority to restore stability and get policies implemented. But they saw the long campaign as a source of uncertainty and a drain on consumer confidence.

HEADLINE: Coalition silent on IR response
INTRO: The Coalition is refusing to release its promised response to the Productivity Commission's workplace relations inquiry, making it increasingly unlikely it will seek support for further industrial relations policy changes at Saturday's election.
TEXT:
The Coalition is refusing to release its promised response to the Productivity Commission's workplace relations inquiry, making it increasingly unlikely it will seek support for further industrial relations policy changes at Saturday's election.

Since the commission's recommendations were released in December 2015, Employment Minister Michaelia Cash has repeatedly promised to provide the Coalition's response before the election. But the Coalition on Wednesday refused to respond directly when asked whether it intended, as promised, to release its response to the commission inquiry before the election.

A Coalition campaign spokeswoman said: "The Coalition has already announced a range of initiatives to provide for fairer and more productive workplaces, including stronger laws to protect vulnerable workers, restore fairness and transparency in workplaces, the restoration of the ABCC, and policies to protect owner-drivers and volunteers firefighters.

"The Coalition's policies include new laws to ban officials of registered organisations from holding office where they repeatedly break the law; prohibitions on corrupting benefits; new disclosure obligations for enterprise agreements; a new public interest test for union mergers; and strong new whistleblower protections."

The commission inquiry was announced before the 2013 election when Tony Abbott and Senator Cash's predecessor, Eric Abetz, wanted to run dead on workplace relations, fearing unions would revive a "return to WorkChoices" style campaign .

Employer groups had hoped the recommendations would be the springboard for the Coalition to advocate significant business-friendly changes to industrial relations policy.

However, the Coalition has been cool on many proposals, concerned support for them would create a voter backlash.

As well as referring the commission's proposed cuts to Sunday penalty rates to the Fair Work Commission, government figures indicated in April the Coalition would not back a contentious proposal for "enterprise contracts" - a new form of contract designed to give small and medium-sized businesses more flexibility to change penalty rates and rosters.

The Australian Financial Review also reported in April the government would not support the inquiry's proposed restructuring of the Fair Work Commission.

But Senator Cash has refused to publicly rule out any recommendations, with business groups saying they were hopeful the Coalition would seek a mandate for other recommendations, including new limits on the content of enterprise agreements.

Australian Mines and Metals Association chief executive Steve Knott said on Wednesday it was "disappointing that both major parties are yet to release substantive workplace relations policies".

"However, the Coalition has a clear agenda," he said.

Finance Minister Mathias Cormann on Wednesday denied union claims the Coalition was hiding its response to the commission recommendations. "We have released policy and there is a few more days to go," he said.

Key points

Senator Michaelia Cash has refused to publicly rule out any recommendations.

The Coalition is concerned about a voter backlash.

HEADLINE: Only leader with agenda to secure prosperity
INTRO: For all Mr Shorten's effective campaigning, Labor remains structurally unfit to govern. In his nine months leading the nation, Mr Turnbull has been too timid in confronting the challenges of securing Australia's modern prosperity. Yet he is the only political leader with both a genuine economic growth agenda and a commitment to reduce the burden of government rather than increase the disincentives of higher taxation. For this newspaper, there is no alternative but to support Mr Turnbull and the Coalition.
TEXT: For all Mr Shorten's effective campaigning, Labor remains structurally unfit to govern. In his nine months leading the nation, Mr Turnbull has been too timid in confronting the challenges of securing Australia's modern prosperity. Yet he is the only political leader with both a genuine economic growth agenda and a commitment to reduce the burden of government rather than increase the disincentives of higher taxation. For this newspaper, there is no alternative but to support Mr Turnbull and the Coalition.

HEADLINE: Victory close, PM seeks more political civility
INTRO: Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull will use his final speech before Saturday's election to call for a new era of civility in politics, saying the culture of "juvenile theatrics and gotcha moments" annoyed voters and hampered efforts to strengthen the economy.
TEXT:
Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull will use his final speech before Saturday's election to call for a new era of civility in politics, saying the culture of "juvenile theatrics and gotcha moments" annoyed voters and hampered efforts to strengthen the economy.

As expectation rapidly builds that the Coalition will be re-elected, Mr Turnbull will argue that Australia's above-average growth rate of 3.1 per cent could not be taken for granted in a volatile global environment.

"Given that uncertainty, my strong sense is that what Australians are looking for most from this election is a step up in political culture - strong, decisive, resolute leadership, yet with a focus on what unites rather than divides," he will tell the National Press Club on Thursday.

Following what has been a relatively civil eight-week election campaign, Labor is now firmly the underdog and is struggling for traction in what has been its worst week of the campaign.

Internal research from both parties, as described to The Australian Financial Review, shows Labor will not gain a single seat in its traditional stronghold of Victoria, so damaging has been the industrial dispute there involving the Country Fire Association.

There is a broad expectation in the party that unless Bill Shorten comes close to winning, Anthony Albanese will nominate for the leadership under a rule that automatically throws the position open following an election loss.

"Everyone's assuming it will be Bill versus Albo," said a source, who added that the NSW Right was backing Mr Shorten.

He said while it was unlikely Labor would win, the party had not given up. "It's not like 2013," he said of Labor's drubbing at the hands of Tony Abbott.

Mr Shorten and Mr Albanese appeared together in Sydney and neither was in the mood to countenance defeat.

"What I want to see on Sunday, I want to get my incoming brief as a minister in a Shorten Labor government. That's my only focus," Mr Albanese said.

Mr Shorten said voters wanted a change in government. "I genuinely observe and discern a mood to change the government and we are going to fight this election right down to 6pm on Saturday night because our issues are biting," he said.

Privately senior sources in both major parties are still worried about the potential for a strong third-party vote, which could create a hung parliament or an unwieldy Senate.

In Victoria, however, where Labor began the campaign targeting at least three Coalition seats, it is now resigned to a holding station at best.

Internal Coalition polling showed the Liberal seat of Dunkley, vacated by retiring popular Liberal Bruce Billson, was set to fall to Labor by 48 per cent to 52 per cent. Now the Coalition's two party-vote is around 53 per cent.

Mr Turnbull will use his speech in Thursday to return to the theme of co-operation and civility that he first called for after he rolled Mr Abbott for the leadership in December.

"One strong sentiment I have picked up from my visits to so many electorates right across the country is this: Australians want the government they elect to get on with the job of ensuring we have a strong economy that can set us up for the future; in uncertain times globally, they are looking for a greater sense of common purpose," he will say.

"I believe they want our Parliament to offload the ideology, to end the juvenile theatrics and gotcha moments, to drop the personality politics.

"They want our focus to be on issues that matter to them and an end to division for division's sake. Australians are entitled to expect that of their Parliament. In these uncertain times, we need to stick together, stick to our economic plan, grow our economy, create more jobs, and build a better future for all Australians. If re-elected on Saturday, that is what I am committed to delivering."

Mr Albanese said Mr Turnbull should stop exploiting Brexit because Brexit showed what happens when you have a weak leader who isn't in control of his party.

"That's what happens when you are so weak that you have a right-wing rump in your party that is dragging you behind, it's like a ball and chain, and you can see it on Turnbull as well. It's not the flu that's causing him the problem. It's the weight that he's carrying. And that's why he's not fit to lead. It's over. They've been there for three years. Abbott was hopeless. Turnbull's been worse. Let's get rid of 'em on Saturday."

HEADLINE: CEOs plead for stability
SUBHEAD: Don't make protest votes, business community urges Hope for a less-obstructionist Senate
INTRO: Leading chief executives and business figures have issued a last-minute plea to voters to avoid a Brexit-style vote for independent and fringe parties that could lead to a hung Parliament and hurt the economy for years.
TEXT:
Leading chief executives and business figures have issued a last-minute plea to voters to avoid a Brexit-style vote for independent and fringe parties that could lead to a hung Parliament and hurt the economy for years.

Support for micro-parties and independents has surged in the lead-up to Saturday's federal election. Polls suggest there may be more independents in the lower house and independent senators such as Pauline Hanson, Jacqui Lambie, Derryn Hinch and Nick Xenophon.

Dozens of business figures, including Asciano CEO and Telstra chairman John Mullen, Wesfarmers CEO Richard Goyder, Woodside Petroleum chairman Michael Chaney and BHP Billiton CEO Andrew Mackenzie, issued the warning to voters.

Former Santos chief executive and chairman of Queensland explorer Blue Energy, John Ellice-Flint, said his message to the voting public as they head to the polls on Saturday was "make your vote count" because Australia couldn't afford three years of a hung Parliament.

"The loss in national productivity in Canberra as a result of a hung Parliament dwarfs most budgetary line items," he said.

Woodside Petroleum and Wesfarmers chairman Michael Chaney said electing independents in a protest vote like the Brexit result would continue ineffective government.

"It is important that governments elected by a majority of the people are able to govern effectively," he said.

Mr Mullen said whichever party was elected, they must be allowed to deliver their policies for the sake of the economy, a suggestion that the Senate not frustrate the incoming government's policies.

"I think the stability of government and the ability to actually deliver on their policies without interference from opposition and minor parties so they can just get on with it, which ever side it is, and then be judged at the end of their period on whether they've done a good job," he said.

"We haven't had it for successive governments because no one has been able to deliver on their policies. Even if you don't agree with the policies it's better for the country if you deliver on them."

Mr Goyder predicted the "script already seems written" for the rise of the independents and former Treasury boss Martin Parkinson's warning last year that we are "sleepwalking into a real mess" was more prescient than ever.

"Come Monday or Tuesday, whoever is in government will pick up the phone to large business and the banks and say we need your help, you are what drives the economy and we need you investing, employing and taking risks, regardless of the rhetoric throughout the election," he said.

The chief executive of Coca-Cola Amatil Australia, Alison Watkins, said her top three priorities for an incoming government were steadily lowering company taxes, becoming a catalyst for the innovation "that will help us become the preferred safe and premium food supplier to Asia" and "making childcare affordable for everyone to drive a more inclusive workplace and society".

Wilson Asset Management chief executive Kate Thorley said that rebuilding confidence after the election would be key.

"Whichever party wins now has a more difficult task ahead," she said. "Businesses are now likely to put spending on hold while they wait for a clearer picture of how the Brexit is going to pan out."

Flight Centre chief executive Graham Turner reflects the growing movement away from the major parties and said he and other business leaders were supporting the Sustainable Australia Party, which wants to reduce immigration.

"If they are successful in the Senate I am happy they will support the lower house government subject to their policies being sustainable for Australia," Mr Turner said.

"Having a sustainable policy on population growth would be the first thing I would suggest mainly by reducing immigration to a more sustainable level of about 70,000 a year from I think more than 200,000 now."

Other business leaders predicted the Brexit fallout would help Malcolm Turnbull clinch victory on Saturday after the prime minister said "a chaotic Labor-Greens-independents alliance would wreck havoc on the economy".

"I think it will help the conservatives," retailer Gerry Harvey said. "One, people are scared of change and two, they've just witnessed change. I've no doubt people will favour the status quo," he said.

Businessman and director Roger Corbett and billionaire poker machine magnate Bruce Mathieson agreed.

"The emphasis in peoples minds will be security - security of jobs and security of superannuation, very clearly that will favour the Coalition. This is not the time for taking risks," Mr Corbett said.

"It will do the Coalition more good than Labor," Mr Mathieson agreed.

Woodside CEO Peter Coleman highlighted the budget, red tape and tax as top of his list for the incoming government.

Australian Foundation Investment Company managing director Ross Barker said the outcome of the election could have a bearing on the Reserve Bank of Australia's interest rate settings in the year ahead.

"A return of the Coalition government, which has committed to continue to rein in spending, may increase the likelihood of another cut to interest rates," he said. "If Labor wins and embarks on a lot of government spending that may ease any short term pressure on the RBA to cut rates."

Mortgage Choice CEO John Flavell said a referendum on an Australian Republic should be a priority for the incoming government.

"With England having made the decision for self-determination in voting to leave the European Union, then my belief is that this is certainly the time for Australians to make our own decision in relation to self-determination.," he said.

HEADLINE: Eyes on ACCC as Woolworths pushes on with hardware exit
INTRO: The clock is ticking on Woolworths' $3 billion exit from the home improvement sector. And a decision by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission on whether Metcash's Mitre 10 should gain clearance to buy Woolworths' Home Timber and Hardware business will have a major impact on the sale process.
TEXT:
The clock is ticking on Woolworths' $3 billion exit from the home improvement sector. And a decision by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission on whether Metcash's Mitre 10 should gain clearance to buy Woolworths' Home Timber and Hardware business will have a major impact on the sale process.

The ACCC's decision is scheduled for Thursday - just four days before final bids for Masters and Home Timber and Hardware are due.

Industry sources believe the ACCC will eventually approve the Metcash/Mitre 10 acquisition, even though it will reduce the number of hardware wholesalers from two to one.

However, the ACCC is expected to delay making a final decision on Thursday and release a statement of issues while it seeks further information about the impact of the merger, which has raised concerns among some Home Timber and hardware members.

A postponement could play into the hands of Blackstone Group, which is offering a "total solution" to Woolworths by bidding for Masters and Home Timber and Hardware.

Blackstone would take on the risk of on-selling Home Timber and Hardware - either to Metcash or rival bidder Anchorage Capital Partners - and the hassle of winding up Masters, liquidating some $1 billion in stock and selling the 60-odd stores and undeveloped sites.

Blackstone's offer would no doubt be appealing to Woolworths, which is said to be keen to agree on a deal before it has to front investors in August.

Charter Hall, which is backed by Bunnings and Harvey Norman, is believed have offered a similar solution.

HEADLINE: Ausgrid suitors seek leaders ahead of auction D-day
INTRO: A key question ahead of final offers being lobbed for a $10 billion stake in NSW's biggest electricity network company, Ausgrid, is who will suitors put forward to run the business should they win?
TEXT:
A key question ahead of final offers being lobbed for a $10 billion stake in NSW's biggest electricity network company, Ausgrid, is who will suitors put forward to run the business should they win?

Sources told Street Talk that over at Cheung Kong Infrastructure a logical choice would be Ben Wilson, the chief of Australian Gas Networks. He is touted as a candidate because he has local knowledge and more than 15 years' experience in utilities banking across Europe, Asia and Latin America.

Wilson is a former director of strategy and regulation and chief financial officer at UK Power Network.

CKI is up against State Grid Corporation of China in the auction, being run by UBS and Deutsche Bank on behalf of the NSW government.

Final offers are due on July 25 ahead of parties presenting detailed business plans to the state government in the following week.

Street Talk this week revealed that Australian Tax Office representatives had flown to Asia to meet with both heavyweight bidders on tax compliance matters.

Elsewhere in the sector, Macquarie Group is understood to have secured Malaysia's retirement vehicle the Employees Provident Fund as a seed investor in its Australian infrastructure fund. The move makes sense given EPF's bigger push into infrastructure investment classes.

Foreign media have reported EPF's chief executive Datuk Shahril Ridza Ridzuan outlining that the fund was aggressively looking at infrastructure assets with the right risk returns and strong cash flows.

EFP is a force to be reckoned with as it has $229 billion in its coffers reflecting the funds of members.

Earlier this year, Street Talk revealed, the group's Macquarie Infrastructure and Real Assets unit had received commitments worth about $400 million for its local infrastructure-targeted fund. That was about one-quarter of the way to its $1.5 billion goal.

HEADLINE: Banks back at Redcape's bar
INTRO: Pub operator Redcape has its appetite back for a possible initial public offering following the breakdown of sale talks with Moelis earlier this year.
TEXT:
Pub operator Redcape has its appetite back for a possible initial public offering following the breakdown of sale talks with Moelis earlier this year.

Investment banks started pitching to Redcape last week for a dual-track process which may result in a trade sale or a stockmarket float later in the second half.

JPMorgan and UBS were working on the original float plan, which was shelved on concerns about market volatility. The two banks are expected to have a second stab at the mandate but rivals, including Lazard (which may be angling for an independent advisory role), are also pitching.

Lazard's co-head in Australia, Lachlan Edwards, is on the board of the real estate investment trust HPI, whose assets include some bottle shops formerly owned by Coles.

Redcape owns 23 pubs in NSW. Its hedge fund owners, York Capital and Varde Partners, are keen to cash out. The dual-track process is expected to kick off in the next two months following a refinancing.

One thing investors in the pubs space will want to consider is what impact anti-gambling senator Nick Xenophon might have on the sector if his party holds the balance of power following Saturday's election.
